The Bolivian tyrannulet (Zimmerius bolivianus) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that align closely with those of other small-bodied Neotropical passerines. Based on data derived from the closely related golden-faced tyrannulet (Zimmerius chrysops), nestlings emerge from the egg at an average age of 17 days [ab = 17 days] when incubated at a mean temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], a developmental period that is modest relative to the 26-day incubation typical of larger tyrant flycatchers. These hatchlings weigh approximately 1.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.2 grams], placing them among the lighter altricial newborns recorded for the Tyrannidae; the thermal conditions of incubation likely impose constraints on metabolic efficiency early in development. The brevity of the embryonic stage reflects a strategy of accelerated maturation within a narrow thermal window, ensuring that chicks hatch before seasonal rains intensify and reduce foraging hours for provisioning adults.

Under the active metabolic conditions typical of this species, characterized by a stable core body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds during the post-hatching period. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], a comparatively rapid transition that reduces the duration of nest vulnerability to predation at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This period is followed by a faster somatic maturation phase: puberty and the onset of gonadal activity are attained at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], suggesting that individuals can become reproductively viable within the same breeding season in which they hatched at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The tight developmental chronology appears to be an adaptation to the short optimal window for breeding in montane cloud forests, where insect prey availability peaks briefly following the wet season.

Turning to reproductive output, under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], with only a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This modest annual fecundity is consistent with the general pattern observed among small insectivorous tyrannids of Andean cloud forests, where extended parental care periods constrain the number of nesting attempts per season. The combination of a small clutch size and a uniparous annual schedule results in a low overall reproductive rate, a life-history strategy that trades high per-offspring investment against numerical output. Such a strategy is viable only when adult survivorship is sufficiently high to offset the low fecundity; indeed, the species' relatively extended lifespan, estimated at about 2628 days since birth [am = about 2628 days since birth], provides the necessary temporal buffer for multiple reproductive attempts across several s at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]easons.

Adult females of Zimmerius bolivianus reach a maximum body mass of approximately 11 grams [Wwi = approximately 11 grams], a value that falls within the range of 10–11.6 grams reported for the species in the literature. This modest adult mass, combined with a hatchling mass of only 1.2 grams, implies a roughly ninefold increase in body size from birth to adulthood, a growth trajectory typical of small-bodied altricial birds. The energy required to sustain this rapid development is considerable. Resting metabolic rates measured under thermoneutral conditions, at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], indicate a basal oxygen consumption of 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This mass-specific metabolic rate is elevated relative to that of larger tyrannids, consistent with the allometric scaling relationship between body size and metabolic intensity, and likely reflects the high energetic demands of thermoregulation and active foraging in the cool, humid environment of the species' high-altitude range.

The first successful reproductive event occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under a maintained body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], indicating that individuals typically delay breeding until their second calendar year, despite having reached puberty by approximately 54 days of age. This year-long gap between the onset of gonadal maturity and actual first reproduction likely reflects the time required to acquire a territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. The deferral of first breeding until an age of 365 days, when the bird has reached its full adult mass of 11 grams, suggests that body size and energetic reserves represent significant constraints on the timing of initial reproductive effort in this cloud-forest specialist.
